idea.name: Airfoil Foundry: an AI-native, owned hot-section casting, coating and repair line for industrial gas turbines (the TSMC of IGT airfoils)
idea.sector: Gas and steam power generation: gas turbine hot-section parts and capacity
idea.one_liner: Build and own the scarce thing in the turbine shortage, a qualified casting, coating and repair line for industrial gas turbine blades and vanes. Use printed ceramic cores and shells and AI solidification control so that one line can run hundreds of reverse-engineered part numbers for 6B, 7EA, 7FA and SGT fleets, and sell parts and repaired sets on long-term supply contracts.
idea.what_it_owns: Three things. (1) The physical capacity: vacuum-induction DS and equiaxed furnaces, ceramic-printing cells, coating booths, braze and HIP, all of it scarce. (2) The frozen, characterised process, a 'PDK' of design rules and process signatures for each alloy and geometry family. (3) A growing library of reverse-engineered technical data packages for orphan and OEM-locked frames. For industrial (non-aviation) turbines there is no FAA or PMA gate. The approver is the asset owner and its insurer, so the company's own evidence record plus customer acceptance is the approval, and it accumulates per part number.
idea.wedge_first_revenue: Months 0-12: hot-gas-path repair and refurbishment on the oldest frames (6B, 7EA, 5002), which needs no casting: AI-planned braze and coating repair, re-tip, recoat, plus reverse-engineered equiaxed nozzles and shrouds produced by partner foundries. Anchor customers are independent service providers and owners of old peakers and resurrection-style fleets, who face OEM parts lead times of 52-80 weeks. First revenue is roughly $2-5M from repaired sets (est.). Months 12-30: commission the first owned equiaxed and DS line using printed cores and shells, which removes the 6-12 month wax and core-die tooling step (est.).
idea.ladder: 1) Repair and refurbish 6B/7EA hot-gas-path sets. 2) Equiaxed stage-2/3 nozzles and buckets from the owned line. 3) DS first-stage buckets for 7EA/7FA. 4) Single-crystal parts for F- and H-class and aeroderivatives. 5) Become the open, characterised 'foundry service' that other designers (new turbine startups, SpaceX-style entrants, the Boom Superpower class) cast into, and the parts supplier to its own turbine fleets.
idea.numbers: Bottleneck: Howmet says it holds more than 50% of the IGT blade market, calls demand 'extraordinary', and says significant new capacity arrives only in 2028-2030 because some equipment takes 2-3+ years (https://www.tikr.com/blog/howmet-aerospace-hwm-stock-drops-elon-musk-turbine-production). One estimate puts a custom DS/SX vacuum-induction furnace at about 1.5 years and purchase order to stable qualified output at 3.5+ years (https://longportapp.cn/topics/39896668). Casting lead times are 52-80 weeks according to a vendor release (https://www.daily-tribune.com/online_features/press_releases/ddm-systems-ceramic-3d-printing-targets-the-gas-turbine-casting-bottleneck-in-ai-data-centers/article_cd7a6cd0-24e0-5113-b0a7-8ffdccc75c12.html). Value of capacity: GE Aerospace agreed to buy Consolidated Precision Products for $11.75B, and SpaceX is building its own blade foundry in Bastrop, TX (https://www.turbomachinerymag.com/view/ge-aerospace-cpp-acquisition-spacex-turbine-blade-foundry). Demand: global turbine orders were 110 GW at end-2025 against 60-70 GW of manufacturing capacity, and turbine prices are heading to about $600/kW by 2027, +195% since 2019 (https://www.power-eng.com/gas/turbines/gas-turbine-prices-climb-195-as-supply-crunch-reshapes-power-development/). Gas turbine services are about $27B in 2025 (https://www.gminsights.com/industry-analysis/gas-turbine-service-market); hot-section parts plus repair are about 30-40% of that, $8-11B (est.). Unit economics (all est.): a 7FA first-stage bucket set costs roughly $1.5-3M from the OEM, and a non-OEM set at 60-70% of OEM price on an owned line runs at 40-50% gross margin. Capital (est.): $5-10M for the repair wedge; $60-150M for the first owned equiaxed/DS line, which is DOE/DPA-fundable as a strategic-capacity case. Time to $100M revenue: about 5-6 years (est.). Ceiling comparables: Howmet (market cap tens of billions, est.), the CPP deal at $11.75B, HEICO, and PCC (sold to Berkshire for $37B in 2016).
idea.ai_role: AI does four jobs. (1) Reverse compilation: CT and blue-light scans, spectroscopy and metallography of worn parts become a TDP with cooling-passage geometry and coating stack. This turns per-part engineering from months into days and makes a library of hundreds of part numbers affordable (P1, P2, P12). (2) A process compiler: physics-informed solidification and grain models plus in-situ thermal and acoustic signatures choose gating, withdrawal rates and core designs, cutting the scrap-and-retry loop that makes casting a 3.5-year ramp (P4, P13). (3) Craft capture: it records master foundry and repair technicians' setups and replays them as procedures and robot motion (P11). (4) An evidence compiler: a per-part digital traveller and a signature-in-envelope acceptance record serve as the qualification package the asset owner and insurer accept.
idea.main_killer: Single-crystal and DS casting yield is tacit, capital-heavy know-how held by three incumbents (Howmet, PCC, and CPP now inside GE). A startup line could take 3.5+ years and $100M+ before it ships qualified parts, and OEMs can threaten LTSA or warranty penalties against owners who install non-OEM hot-section parts.
idea.ai_answer_to_killer: Climb the hardness ladder instead of starting at single-crystal. Repair and equiaxed parts need far less tacit yield knowledge and earn money in year 1. Printed ceramic cores and shells (Lithoz cells are already in Safran production for blade cores, https://www.lithoz.com/en/lithoz-has-installed-cerafab-s65-printers-to-build-casting-parts-for-safran-aircraft-engines/) remove tooling lead time, and AI solidification models plus per-pour signatures compress the learn-by-scrap ramp. Many units per mould and active-learning test design mean each pour is an experiment. The OEM threat does not apply to the target customers: 6B/7EA fleets are mostly out of LTSA, and independent service providers and resurrection fleets want a second source. Industrial turbines have no regulator queue, so the evidence gate is the owner's, and the company can be its own first customer by supplying a sister firm-power fleet.
idea.competitors: Casting: Howmet, PCC Airfoils (Berkshire), CPP (being acquired by GE Aerospace), Doncasters, Chromalloy (Veritas). Repair and independent service providers: Chromalloy, EthosEnergy, PSM (Hanwha), Sulzer, MTU. OEM captive: GE Vernova, Siemens Energy, MHI. New entrants: SpaceX's in-house foundry; DDM Systems (printed ceramic shells); Lithoz and 3DCeram (core printing tools, which are suppliers rather than competitors).
idea.principles_used: P1 (own the frozen target, not the compiler), P3 (owned qualified capacity), P11 (abundant designers, scarce qualified cell), P12 (break the OEM parts lock), P13 (portable recipe plus envelope), P14 (no FAA gate for industrial turbines; owner and insurer are the gate)

In short, the first rungs earn modest money and the rungs that earn real money arrive late and may be locked.

(3) Incumbents can copy the edge. Printed cores (Lithoz in Safran production) and solidification ML can be bought by Howmet, PCC and GE-CPP, who also have far more pour data. Incumbents have already ordered ahead in the vacuum-furnace vendor queue. Their new capacity lands around 2028-30, roughly when the startup's owned line would qualify, so the shortage premium may fade just as the line comes online. New H-class units sit under 10-20 year OEM LTSAs, so the open aftermarket is mainly the ageing E/F fleet.

Each problem has an AI-leveraged answer, so none is fatal. But the pitch as written ('repair 6B/7EA, then climb') walks straight into PE-owned ISPs on their home turf.

verdicts.what_survives:
The strongest version is a quick-turn, high-mix foundry, not a repair shop.

Incumbent foundries (Howmet, PCC, GE-CPP) put their furnace time into high-volume aero contracts and new-build OEM IGT. The low-volume, high-part-count aftermarket of orphan and out-of-LTSA E/F-class frames gets little of that capacity. That aftermarket covers stage 2-3 nozzles, shrouds, transition-piece hardware and DS stage-1 buckets for 6B, 7EA, 7FA, SGT-800 and similar frames, and it waits 52-80 weeks.

The AI edge is fewer weeks per part number. Reverse-compile a scan into a TDP in days, print the cores and shells with no hard tooling, run a physics-informed process recipe, and treat every pour as an experiment. That makes it economic to cast batches of 20-200 that incumbents decline.

Go to market:
- Sell first to the ISPs themselves (PSM, EthosEnergy, Allied, small shops), who lack casting capacity, and to resurrection-style fleets and the new merchant peaker builders. Do not sell repair against them.
- Use repair or refurbishment only as a cash bridge, bought rather than built: acquire one small regional repair shop.
- Take DOE/DPA strategic-capacity funding for the first equiaxed/DS line.

Defensibility comes from three things, and only if speed holds:
- a per-part-number acceptance record with owners and insurers;
- the qualified PDK (frozen design rules and process data per alloy and geometry family);
- being the open casting foundry for new turbine entrants (Boom-class, data-centre self-builders) that do not want to depend on GE-owned CPP.

Revised scores:
- N 4: the economics hold while the shortage lasts.
- T 3: the owned line qualifies at month 30 or later.
- C 5: comparables are PCC at $37B and CPP at $11.75B.
- A 4: printed tooling plus solidification ML answers the 3.5-year ramp.
- D 3, down from 4: incumbents can buy the same printers, have more pour data, and already hold decades of reverse-engineered libraries; what is left is speed and the high-mix niche.

Total 19, a narrow pass. The pitch must drop 'repair first against Chromalloy/PSM/EthosEnergy' and lead with 'we cast the parts the ISPs and new turbine builders cannot get'.

verdicts.fatal_issue: No single fatal issue. The gates that control the clock are physical and evidential, not regulatory, and AI only partly shortens them. (1) Equipment queue: vacuum DS/SX furnaces, EB-PVD/LPPS coaters and HIP all have 1.5-3 year lead times. The startup waits in the same supplier queue as Howmet and PCC, and AI does not move it. (2) Customer qualification depends on fleet operating hours. Utilities and their property insurers accept non-OEM first-stage DS buckets only after a lead unit has run about one hot-gas-path interval: roughly 24k equivalent hours on baseload, which is about 3 years, or 900-1,200 starts on peakers, which takes longer. No model compresses that clock. A sister peaker fleet helps little because peakers log few hours. (3) Ceiling. IGT hot-section parts plus repair is about $8-11B (est.). The PCC, Howmet and CPP comparables are mostly aero, which sits behind the FAA/PMA gate this idea avoids. So the IGT-only version is a credible $1-5B company, not a clear $10B+ one, and C drops from 5 to 4. (4) The shortage window may close: Howmet/PCC capacity lands in 2028-30, just as the owned DS line would qualify. (5) The repair wedge is crowded (Chromalloy, EthosEnergy, PSM/Hanwha, Sulzer, Liburdi, Allied Power Group). In a shortage it is also limited by the supply of serviceable used parts to repair, not only by labour.

idea.name: Keel Forge: an AI-characterised naval castings and forgings foundry, bought, not built
idea.one_liner: Acquire PE-held or family-owned foundries and forge shops that already hold NAVSEA and prime approvals, turn each into an AI-characterised 'frozen target' with in-situ process signatures, and own the scarce capacity for the large castings and forgings that gate submarine, ship and ground-vehicle repair.
idea.sector: Defence sustainment (naval and ground-vehicle hot-section and structural castings and forgings)
idea.what_it_owns: The scarce physical capacity (melt shops, presses, heat-treat, NDT). The approvals and qualified-supplier status that come with the acquired plants (NAVSEA Level I/SUBSAFE-adjacent, ASME, prime AVLs). A process design kit per plant: published design rules and ML process signatures that make each line a characterised, compilable target. A library of patterns and recipes for out-of-production repair and spare castings.
idea.wedge_first_revenue: Revenue starts on day one by buying a foundry or forge with an existing defence backlog. The AI wedge is yield and cycle time: solidification simulation, gating and risering design, and in-process sensing to cut scrap and rework on large steel, bronze and nickel-aluminium-bronze castings where first-pass yield is poor. That raises throughput from capacity already approved, so no new approval is needed.
idea.ladder: 1) Acquire one approved foundry and raise yield and on-time delivery. 2) Roll up 3-6 more (hundreds of US foundries have closed and many are founder- or PE-owned), so pattern and recipe libraries move across plants under one quality system (P13 portable recipes). 3) Open a 'MOSIS for castings' service: the Navy's maintenance centres and primes send repair-part designs to a published design-rule target and get qualified castings in weeks. 4) Own spare and rotable inventory of long-lead castings and sell them on availability contracts to the public shipyards and depots. 5) The TSMC of large metal parts for defence.
idea.numbers: Pain: submarine and ship maintenance is late largely because of long-lead castings and forgings; lead times of about 2-3+ years on large castings are reported (est.). Congress has put est. $10B+ into the submarine industrial base since about 2018. The Abrams fleet's maintenance cost rose $181.3M from FY2015 to FY2023 (https://www.gao.gov/products/GAO-26-108113 ; https://news.usni.org/2025/09/25/gao-report-on-weapon-system-sustainment). US foundries: about 1,700 operating, down from more than 3,000 decades ago (est.). Asset prices: small foundries often trade at about 4-7x EBITDA (est.). idea.name: RAID Power: a redundant array of inexpensive engines, an owned firm-power fleet built from mass-produced gas engine modules
idea.sector: Gas and steam power generation: distributed firm power (reciprocating gas engines) for data centers and industry
idea.one_liner: Do to the heavy-frame gas turbine what Google's commodity servers did to the mainframe. Own thousands of hot-swappable 0.5-2 MW natural-gas engine modules built on high-volume engine blocks, orchestrated by software into N+k firm-power plants, and sell guaranteed firm power, not boxes.
idea.what_it_owns: The fleet: generating modules, sites, air permits and gas interconnects. A central robotic remanufacturing depot, the 'factory' that maintenance becomes. Long-term firm-power and capacity contracts. And the fleet's operating-history dataset, which sets its cost of debt (P10). Reliability is a property of the array and its software, not of any one machine, so the company is the approver of its own availability guarantee.
idea.wedge_first_revenue: Bridge and behind-the-meter power for 20-100 MW data-center and industrial loads stuck in 5-7 year interconnection queues, billed as $/MW-month capacity plus a fuel pass-through. First 10-20 MW use bought-in gensets on modern heavy-duty natural-gas truck and industrial engine blocks with three-way-catalyst aftertreatment, deployed within 6-9 months against 12-18 months for large reciprocating engines and 5+ years for frames. Year-1 revenue is roughly $5-15M (est.).
idea.ladder: 1) Bridge power fleets. 2) Permanent behind-the-meter firm power with heat recovery to absorption chillers. 3) Its own standardised 'frozen target' module design, sourcing blocks from automotive-scale lines so Wright's law applies (P5). 4) Grid capacity resource: aggregated arrays bid into PJM/ERCOT capacity and reserve markets. 5) Fuel-flexible modules (hydrogen blends, RNG) and export to emerging-market grids as 'power in a container'. 6) Securitised firm-power contract book at infrastructure spreads.
idea.numbers: Shortage: global turbine orders of 110 GW against 60-70 GW of capacity, six-year lead times, equipment prices heading to about $600/kW (+195% since 2019) (https://www.power-eng.com/gas/turbines/gas-turbine-prices-climb-195-as-supply-crunch-reshapes-power-development/). Recent US combined-cycle projects cost about $2,000/kW (https://www.publicpower.org/periodical/article/new-report-finds-rising-cost-new-gas-plants-outpacing-planning-assumptions). Large reciprocating engines quote 12-18 months against 5+ years for heavy frame (https://www.marketsandmarkets.com/Market-Reports/data-center-onsite-behind-the-meter-power-market-129738654.html). Caterpillar's backlog is about $63B, its large-engine backlog is up 3.5x since January 2024, and it plans to triple capacity (https://www.fool.com/investing/2026/08/03/caterpillars-order-backlog-hit-a-record-63-billion/ ; https://www.manufacturingdive.com/news/caterpillar-triple-power-generation-capacity-raises-2030-targets-q1-2026-earnings/). Hyperscale orders for engine-based power are now 400-800 MW each, e.g. Wärtsilä 412 MW in Ohio and 790 MW in Texas, and Everllence 480 MW (https://pgjonline.com/news/2026/april/waertsilae-to-supply-412-mw-of-gas-fired-power-for-us-data-center ; https://www.modernpowersystems.com/news/everllence-secures-480-mw-gas-engine-contract-for-us-hyperscale-data-centre/). Grid interconnection averages about 5 years (https://www.pew.org/de/research-and-analysis/articles/2026/02/09/to-harness-power-plants-unused-capacity-states-can-turn-to-surplus-interconnection-service). Unit economics (all est.): installed cost $600-900/kW for an array of volume modules against $1,200-2,000/kW for large reciprocating engines or CCGT. Contract price $25-40/kW-month for firm capacity plus fuel; about 25-35% unlevered project IRR in a supply-short market, converging to 12-15%. Capital: $1M-ish per MW (est.); project debt after 24-36 months of history. Time to $100M revenue: about 3-4 years (est.) at roughly 150-250 MW contracted. Ceiling comparables: Bloom Energy (owned and leased firm power for data centers, market cap tens of billions in 2026, est.), Enchanted Rock, United Rentals, Aggreko (bought for about £2.3B in 2021).
idea.ai_role: AI does four jobs. (1) Fleet orchestration as the 'scheduler', the RAID controller: it dispatches modules for load-following, keeps N+k redundancy and rotates wear so the array delivers higher availability than any single unit (P3, P8). (2) Per-module self-models: ML on vibration, exhaust and oil analysis predicts failures and triggers a hot swap before an outage, turning maintenance from field labour into a scheduled swap plus depot remanufacture (P9). (3) Craft capture in the depot: AI-guided teardown, inspection and rebuild at line speed (P11). (4) Evidence and finance: telemetry becomes the availability record that lenders and insurers price, compressing the cost of capital (P10, P14). It also automates air-permit modelling and paperwork across many sites.
idea.main_killer: Physics and permits. Small engines run at about 35-40% electrical efficiency against about 45-50% for large reciprocating engines and about 60% for CCGT, so fuel cost per MWh is higher. Many small stacks complicate air permits in nonattainment areas. Maintenance hours per MW scale with module count. Wärtsilä, Caterpillar, Bloom and well-funded developers may out-scale the startup.
idea.ai_answer_to_killer: (a) Efficiency: in data-center behind-the-meter use the comparison is not CCGT but no power for 5 years. Firm power is priced on capacity, and heat recovery to absorption cooling replaces chiller electricity, taking effective efficiency to 60-70% (est.). AI dispatch keeps modules at their best-efficiency point instead of part-loading a big machine. (b) Emissions: rich-burn plus three-way catalyst, truck-style, reaches very low NOx, and AI closed-loop air-fuel control holds it per module. That turns the permit into an advantage, and AI can generate permit modelling for each site in days. (c) Maintenance: the hot-swap plus central robotic remanufacture model converts linear field labour into factory throughput, which is exactly the per-unit labour AI collapses. (d) Incumbents sell boxes with 12-18 month lead times. The startup sells owned output and buys blocks from automotive-scale supply that is not sold out.
idea.competitors: Engine OEMs selling equipment: Caterpillar, Wärtsilä, INNIO Jenbacher, Cummins, Everllence, Rolls-Royce mtu, Generac. Owned and operated firm power: Bloom Energy (fuel cells), Enchanted Rock (gas microgrids), VoltaGrid (Jenbacher-based mobile power), Aggreko, APR Energy, ProEnergy, FTAI Power (CFM56-derived 25 MW units, https://distributionstrategy.com/2026/01/ftai-aviation-moves-into-data-center-power-leveraging-engine-distribution-and-mro-platform/), Mainspring (linear generators).
idea.principles_used: P3 (pooled, owned capacity behind an API), P5 (Wright's law on a standard module), P8 (software-defined fleet performance), P9 (fleet telemetry as evidence), P10 (output-as-a-service as a financing technology), P13 (the module is a container: certify once, deploy anywhere)

idea.name: Orphan Silicon Works: the qualified foundry for obsolete military electronics
idea.one_liner: An owned, trusted production line that decompiles obsolete circuit cards, ASICs and avionics boxes into modern form-fit-function replacements (re-synthesised onto current FPGAs and parts) and owns the resulting TDPs, approvals and the only qualified source.
idea.sector: Defence and aerospace sustainment (DMSMS, obsolete electronics)
idea.what_it_owns: A characterised, frozen manufacturing target: the 'PDK for legacy electronics', a qualified board-and-module line (IPC-A-610 Class 3, AS9100, DMEA Trusted Accreditation, ITAR). It also owns a growing library of FFF replacement designs with company-generated data rights, since they are clean-room re-implementations, not copies of OEM data. Over time it holds DLA source approvals and QPL/QML listings on those part numbers, plus last-time-buy die and component inventory. It sells the physical part, not engineering services.
idea.wedge_first_revenue: Begin with buyers who can approve the replacement themselves, so the DLA queue is not on the critical path: (a) contractor-operated and civil-registered operators of ex-military types (including Ghost Wing-style fleets), (b) foreign military users of US-origin platforms, whose national airworthiness authority approves, (c) Navy and Army engineering support activities using emergency or Section 803-style FFF substitution for parts with zero bids, and (d) OEM primes with DMSMS line-stoppages, who buy a qualified replacement module for their own program. First revenue is a replacement CCA or LRU on a known-dead part with long backorders, at a fixed unit price.
idea.ladder: 1) 20-50 high-pain FFF boards for operators who self-approve. 2) Submit the same designs as DLA alternate-source and SAR packages; AI-drafted packages let it file hundreds a year, so the queue runs in parallel. 3) An 'emulation core' family: a few qualified FPGA/SoC modules that emulate thousands of dead legacy chips (the Phoenix BIOS move for avionics), each a frozen, characterised target. 4) Program-level DMSMS sustainment contracts (performance-based logistics) for whole avionics suites. 5) The default second source for legacy US and allied electronics, the HEICO of defence electronics.
idea.numbers: Pain: obsolescence costs the US military 'hundreds of millions of dollars each year' by older DoD-linked estimates (https://acqnotes.com/acqnote/careerfields/diminishing-manufacturing-sources-and-material-shortages), and that undercounts readiness loss. The F/A-22 alone ran about $100M/yr of DMS management (https://www.navsea.navy.mil/Portals/103/Documents/NSWC_Crane/SD-18/PDFs/Resources/ResourcesDMSMS.pdf). Virginia-class logged about 1,440 DMSMS issues since 2001 (https://www.dsp.dla.mil/Portals/26/Documents/Publications/Journal/140701-DSPJ-01.pdf). Sole-source pricing: DoD IG found TransDigm part profits from 17% to over 4,000%, with more than 75% of its net sales sole-source (https://fortune.com/2019/05/15/transdigm-pentagon-gouging ; https://www.bloombergquint.com/business/pentagon-rips-transdigm-for-gouging-with-4-361-half-inch-pin). Addressable market (est.): legacy defence electronics spares and repair at about $15-25B/yr globally. Unit economics (est.): an FFF board sells at $5-50k with 50-65% gross margin. AI cuts per-design engineering from about $150-500k to about $20-60k, so break-even falls to about 20-50 units per design. Capital: $15-30M for a trusted SMT and test line plus a reverse-engineering lab (est.). Time to $100M revenue: about 5-7 years with 1,000+ designs in the library (est.). Ceiling comparables: HEICO Electronic Technologies Group; Rochester Electronics (private, largest authorised EOL semi source); TransDigm's sole-source model.
idea.ai_role: Reverse compilation is the core of the business. X-ray CT and delayering produce netlists. ML infers behaviour from in-circuit test captures. LLM and HDL agents re-synthesise legacy logic (TTL, PALs, dead ASICs) onto current FPGAs, and AI generates equivalence test benches that run the old box and the new box side by side over millions of vectors. Electronics is the one sustainment domain where software's cheap verification partly survives: the replacement can be checked by running it. AI also writes SAR, alternate-source and qualification packages at volume and ranks the 5M+ DLA NSNs by backorder pain and price gap. Laws used: P1 (own the frozen target), P4 (checking cheaper than changing), P6 and P12 (interface clone plus owned approval), P7 (signed equivalences).
idea.main_killer: The gatekeeper queue: DLA source approval takes 12-18 months per part, and engineering support activities are understaffed. OEM primes defend data rights and may push programs to refuse non-OEM boards. Volume per part number is tiny.
idea.ai_answer_to_killer: Don't wait on one queue. Sell first to buyers who are their own approver (contractor operators, foreign militaries, primes with line-down problems), and file AI-generated alternate-source packages in bulk so hundreds of approvals mature in parallel; the queue is a pipeline, not a wall. Solve the volume problem with emulation-core modules: one qualified hardware platform reconfigured in firmware for many dead parts, so qualification evidence on the platform carries over and each new part needs only a functional equivalence proof. Clean-room reimplementation from behaviour avoids OEM data rights, and the 2025-26 DoD push on right-to-repair and data rights in acquisition reform works in its favour.
idea.competitors: Rochester Electronics (EOL semis), GDCA, Spectrum Control, Mercury Systems, Cyient/Teledyne repair, HEICO ETG, and the OEMs' own obsolescence groups. Government depots (NSWC Crane, Warner Robins) reverse-engineer in-house. Startups: Firestorm ($82M reported, unverified, additive), and Hadrian ($1.37B at $7.9B, Aug 2026) in metal parts, not electronics (https://thenextweb.com/news/hadrian-1-37bn-series-d-7-87bn-defence-factories).
idea.principles_used: P1, P4, P6, P7, P12 (also P13 portable recipes)

Weak points, in order:

(1) The market figure is wrong in kind. The $15-25B/yr for "legacy defence electronics spares and repair" has no source. The reachable piece is much smaller. Prior project research found that OEMs (Boeing, GE and others) hold about 83% of DoD sole-source spend, which leaves a reachable DLA long tail of about $0.6-1.2B across all commodities, and electronics is only part of that. Most repair spend sits in organic depots (NSWC Crane, Warner Robins), and those depots reverse-engineer parts themselves.

(2) Revenue per part is small and the clock is set by the government. An approved part earns about $100-150k/yr. $100M of revenue therefore needs about 700-1,000 approved NSNs actually producing revenue, not 1,000 designs sitting in a library. DLA's own figure for source approval is 12-18 months (NDIA 2023), and GAO found under 10% of DLA reverse-engineering projects were completed. AI can write SAR packages in bulk, but DLA and the engineering support activities review them at human speed. On the project's own law, AI fixes per-unit paperwork, not gatekeeper queues. Filing hundreds of packages does not make the reviewers approve hundreds a year.

(3) The pricing model does not carry over. TransDigm earns 17% to 4,000% because its OEM parts are designed into the platform and it holds the data rights. A second-source part sold to DLA is competed on price: DLA re-competes, and a breakout cuts the margin, as the PSM case cut GE 7FA part prices 60-70%. The FFF line keeps its margin only while it is the sole approved source. AI also makes the next reverse-engineering effort cheap for rivals and for the depots (the law that AI levels knowledge for everyone).

(4) Qualification, not engineering, drives the cost per design. AI can cut design NRE to $20-60k, but a Class 3 avionics LRU still needs first-article, ESS and MIL-STD-810 / DO-160-class environmental and EMI testing, often $100-500k. That puts break-even at 50-200+ units, not 20-50, and many dead NSNs sell only 5-50 units a year.

(5) The self-approving wedge is real but small. Contractor-operated ex-military fleets are a few hundred aircraft. Foreign users often buy through FMS (so the US service still decides) or defer to the US engineering authority, and direct sales need ITAR DSP-5 licences. I put this wedge at about $20-60M/yr reachable (est.).

(6) The direct comparables are acquisition-sized. Innovasic (emulation of obsolete chips) went to Analog Devices (memory). GDCA and Lansdale are small private niches. The $1B+ comparable that does exist, HEICO ETG (about $1.2B in sales, memory), got there by buying dozens of niche electronics companies, not by building organically.

verdicts.what_survives: The strongest version: be the OEM of record by buying the approval, then use AI to make it pay. The idea should not start by filing DLA alternate-source packages or by selling FFF boards to primes, which is a service. Instead, buy orphaned avionics and defence-electronics product lines, with their type designs, source approvals, NSNs, CAGE codes and the installed base, from OEMs and primes that want to exit low-volume legacy lines. This is the HEICO/TransDigm acquisition playbook, and sellers often treat these lines as a nuisance, so they may price low rather than in hope. As OEM of record, the company is already the approved source, so the DLA queue and the prime-as-approver problem go away for those part numbers: 'be your own approver' by acquisition. AI then answers the killer, which is that these lines die because their dead parts make them uneconomic to keep building. HDL and test-bench agents re-implement the dead ICs and boards inside the owned design, and running old and new boxes side by side gives digital-equivalence evidence, filed as OEM-internal Class II changes rather than new-source approvals. The 'emulation core' should be built only as an internal platform, because Innovasic/ADI holds that rung as a merchant product. Revenue is the physical spares and repair of owned part numbers at sole-source pricing. The clean-room library and AI-drafted DLA packages become secondary growth channels. Weaknesses that remain: it is capital-heavier (acquisitions, roughly $50-150M debt plus equity over time), it is close to a PE roll-up model (Arcline, HEICO and TransDigm compete for the same lines), and the analog/RF parts still need conventional engineering. With the acquire-the-approval wedge, plausible scores are N3-4, T3-4, C4-5 (TransDigm/HEICO comparables), A3 and D4, about 17-19. Run as written (startup-filed approvals plus selling to primes), it scores about 16 and fails the bar without being fatally refuted.

verdicts.fatal_issue: I found no fatal issue, but the idea drops below the 19/25 pass line. The binding gate is not the DLA SAR queue. It is the qualification and airworthiness evidence each replacement must carry, and the company sits inside that gate. A re-synthesised FPGA replacement of a flight- or mission-critical card or LRU still needs (a) environmental and EMI qualification (MIL-STD-810/461-type vibration, thermal, EMI, run in calendar-bound third-party labs; AI does not shorten this), (b) complex-electronic-hardware assurance that a service technical airworthiness authority (NAVAIR, the USAF airworthiness office, the Army's AMRDEC/DEVCOM) will accept, and (c) ESA or program-office configuration-control sign-off. No regulator yet accepts AI-generated equivalence testing in place of these. Running old and new boxes side by side over millions of vectors is strong engineering evidence, but it is not accepted proof for state-heavy logic with timing, metastability or SEU behaviour. Two more problems. The 'emulation core' move already exists as government property: DLA's GEM (Generalized Emulation of Microcircuits) program and DMEA's own foundry and ATSP reverse-engineering line supply FFF obsolete microcircuits and boards to DoD at cost. So the highest-pain government parts have an in-house competitor that is also the approver. The 'self-approving buyer' wedge is also smaller than claimed. Foreign users of US-origin platforms need USG/ITAR authorisation to modify or replace configuration items and often defer to the US program office. Contractor-operated ex-military fleets number in the low hundreds of aircraft.

verdicts.what_survives:
Revised scores: N3, T3, C4, A3, D4 = 17. It does not pass, but it is not refuted.

What survives is a narrower and sharper version: 'buy the approvals, then AI-multiply them.'

1) Acquire one or two small existing approved-source / DMSMS houses that already hold DLA CAGE approvals, QML/QPL listings, AS9100, ITAR and DMEA trusted accreditation on dozens to hundreds of NSNs. Such firms are often founder-owned at small revenue, in the GDCA/Lansdale/Innovasic class. This is the 'be your own approver / buy the ODA' move. It converts the 12-18 month queue into an owned starting stock and puts first revenue in year 1.

2) Qualify ONE emulation-core hardware family environmentally and for EMI once, as a ruggedised drop-in CCA form factor. Each new dead part then becomes a firmware variant needing only functional equivalence plus qualification-by-similarity. AI's real job is cutting per-variant reverse-engineering and equivalence-test cost toward ~$20-60k, enough to compete with GEM/DMEA on speed and breadth rather than price.

3) Target non-flight-critical and naval/ground mission electronics first: ship combat-system cards, radar and sonar processors, ground vehicles, test equipment and ATE, munitions test sets. There, ESA approval is engineering judgment, and airworthiness DAL-style assurance is not on the critical path. Sell to primes with line-down DMSMS problems as their qualified supplier, so the prime's program office does the approving.

4) Use AI at scale where it truly beats incumbents. Rank NSNs by backorder pain against a price gap that GEM/DMEA do not cover. Mass-produce SAR and alternate-source packages as a parallel pipeline (upside, not the plan).

Defensibility is real: each approved NSN is a sticky sole-source annuity, and the qualified platform's evidence carries across parts. The ceiling is credible at $1B+ via the HEICO-ETG path. Main residual risks:
- Government in-house emulation (GEM/DMEA) takes the best parts.
- Sole-source cost-data scrutiny caps margins below the TransDigm level.
- Flight-critical avionics LRUs stay gated by airworthiness evidence that AI cannot yet substitute.

idea.name: Gridright: an interconnection-rights fleet that buys retiring coal and steam plants for their grid rights and repowers them with gas
idea.sector: Gas and steam power generation: brownfield repowering (steam turbines, boilers, HRSGs) and grid interconnection
idea.one_liner: The scarcest permission in power is a grid connection, which takes about 5 years to get new. Buy mid-size retiring coal and old gas-steam plants for their capacity interconnection rights and existing steam turbines, repower them fast (boiler gas conversion first, then gas turbine plus HRSG to make combined cycle), and sell capacity and firm power to the grid and co-located loads.
idea.what_it_owns: Capacity interconnection rights, which are portable to replacement generation under PJM's 2026 fast track and FERC surplus interconnection rules. The sites, water rights, rail and transmission yards. Existing steam turbine-generators and switchyards. An AI-built steam-plant parts and records library. And the repowered generating fleet with its capacity contracts. This is the 'own the permission' shape: the interconnection is the approval nobody can copy.
idea.wedge_first_revenue: Target 50-400 MW units owned by co-ops, munis and small IPPs, which big PE ignores. Close before retirement and file as a PJM Replacement Generation Resource, or keep the 1-year surplus-interconnection clock alive. First repower is a coal-to-gas boiler conversion of the existing steam unit (about 12-18 months, est.) that clears the capacity auction. At the $333/MW-day cap, a 200 MW unit earns about $24M a year of capacity revenue alone, before energy (est. from PJM cap).
idea.ladder: 1) Gas-convert existing boilers and sell capacity and energy. 2) Add aeroderivative or used frame gas turbines plus HRSGs feeding the existing steam turbine (repowered combined cycle). 3) Co-locate data centers or industrial loads behind the point of interconnection under surplus interconnection service (storage, solar). 4) A rollup of 20-40 sites, 5-10 GW, becoming a mid-cap IPP. 5) Later, advanced-nuclear or SMR replacement at the same rights, since coal-to-nuclear sites carry DOE and state support.
idea.numbers: Queue: average about 5 years from proposal to grid connection (https://www.pew.org/de/research-and-analysis/articles/2026/02/09/to-harness-power-plants-unused-capacity-states-can-turn-to-surplus-interconnection-service). On Jan 29, 2026 FERC accepted PJM's fast-track for Replacement Generation Resources that assume capacity interconnection rights from retiring generators; surplus interconnection service may continue at most 1 year after retirement (https://www.troutmanenergyreport.com/?p=13304 ; https://www.iso-ne.com/static-assets/documents/100031/a03_tc_surplus_interconnection_service_presentation.pdf ; https://www.mcguirewoods.com/client-resources/alerts/2025/2/ferc-approves-expansion-of-pjms-surplus-interconnection-service-to-address-near-term-resource-adequacy-concerns). Prices: PJM capacity cleared at the $333.44/MW-day cap (would have been $529.80 uncapped), and the 2027/28 auction is about $16.4B (per P3). New CCGT costs about $2,000/kW (https://www.publicpower.org/periodical/article/new-report-finds-rising-cost-new-gas-plants-outpacing-planning-assumptions), and turbine slots extend to 2029-2031 (https://www.turbomachinerymag.com/view/steam-turbines-gas-turbine-bottleneck-siemens-energy). Precedent: Homer City (PA's largest coal plant) is being redeveloped as a 4.5 GW gas-powered data-center campus (https://abcnews.go.com/amp/Technology/wireStory/pennsylvanias-largest-coal-fired-power-plant-now-retired-120412657). Unit economics (est.): coal-to-gas boiler conversion about $50-200/kW; repowered combined cycle reusing the steam turbine and switchyard about $800-1,200/kW against $2,000/kW greenfield; site acquisition often $0-100/kW plus assumed decommissioning liabilities. Capital: $20-50M equity for first site plus project debt (est.). Time to $100M revenue: about 3 years at 2-3 sites (est.). Ceiling comparables: Vistra, NRG, Talen and Constellation (IPP market caps of tens of billions, est.).
idea.ai_role: AI does four jobs. (1) Underwriting the long tail: it ingests EIA-860 data, ISO queue data, retirement notices, plant permits and transmission studies to rank every unit in the US by repower value and interconnection headroom. This is per-deal labour that today only big IPPs staff (P2, P7). (2) Reverse compilation of the plant: decades of paper drawings, P&IDs, turbine overhaul records and boiler inspection reports become a digital plant model in weeks, so repower engineering and permitting packages can be drafted for each site (P1, P4). (3) A steam-turbine parts library for 1960s-90s GE, Westinghouse and Allis-Chalmers units, reverse-engineered as in P12. (4) Control retrofits and fleet tuning: new controls on old units for ramp rate and minimum load (P8), with operating telemetry as the evidence for capacity accreditation (P9).
idea.main_killer: First rungs are held by funded players and sellers price in hope. Vistra, NRG, Constellation, PE (Knighthead, LS Power) and hyperscalers are all hunting coal sites. DOE 202(c) orders and utilities keep some coal plants open. Sites carry environmental liabilities (ash ponds, CCR rules).
idea.ai_answer_to_killer: Go where the big buyers cannot look economically: the hundreds of 50-400 MW co-op, muni and small-IPP units across PJM, MISO and SERC. AI makes per-site diligence close to zero marginal cost, so the startup can screen and bid on every one, beating PE's analyst throughput. Structure the deal as a rights purchase plus a liability-assumption contract where sellers (co-ops facing closure costs) value relief from ash-pond and decommissioning liabilities more than price. AI-driven environmental characterisation and remediation planning prices those liabilities better than the seller can. 202(c) is an upside: units kept running preserve their rights while the repower is prepared.
idea.competitors: IPPs: Vistra, NRG, Constellation, Talen. PE and developers: LS Power, Knighthead (Homer City), Hull Street Energy, Earthrise Energy (coal-to-clean). Hyperscalers buying sites directly. Utilities self-repowering. Renewable developers using surplus interconnection at coal sites. Nuclear site developers (TerraPower's Kemmerer coal site).
idea.principles_used: P6 and P12 (own the right to substitute: the interconnection is the interface), P14 (owner-operator is its own gate inside the fence), P8 (control-layer uplift on orphaned assets), P9 (operating history for capacity accreditation), P2 (an AI-built library for an orphaned steam fleet)

verdicts.fatal_issue:
Nothing fatal, but the pitched numbers are too high. Caveat on method: every web search was refused because the 200-search budget for this turn was already used up, so I could not rebuild anything from fresh primary sources. The rebuild below uses the URLs cited in the idea plus public facts I knew as of mid-2026. Each of those facts is marked 'from memory' and should be checked in a follow-up search turn.

What breaks in the numbers is the claim of 'very high site IRRs at $24M/yr capacity per 200 MW'. Four things cut that down.

(1) Accreditation haircut. PJM pays capacity on accredited MW (ELCC-adjusted UCAP), not nameplate. A gas-fired steam unit accredits at roughly 60-80% (from memory). So 200 MW nameplate is about 150 MW UCAP, which earns about $18M/yr at the $333/MW-day cap, not $24M.

(2) Fixed costs on an old steam unit. Fixed O&M runs about $40-60/kW-yr, or $8-12M/yr. That eats half the capacity revenue.

(3) Thin energy margin. At a heat rate of about 10,500 Btu/kWh, a converted boiler is a low-capacity-factor peaker. Energy margin is maybe $3-6M/yr.

(4) The gas lateral. Many coal sites have no firm gas supply, and a pipeline lateral can cost $20-100M+. That can be bigger than the conversion itself ($10-40M).

Net: EBITDA is about $10-15M/yr on $60-100M all-in cost. That is a 12-20% unlevered yield, but only while capacity sits near the cap. The cap is a negotiated collar (Shapiro settlement for 2026/27-2027/28; extension pushed by the White House and governors in early 2026, from memory), not a market fundamental. At $150/MW-day, EBITDA falls to about $3-5M and the asset returns about 5%. So capacity-price persistence is the real numbers risk.

Supply is also thinner than the pitch assumes. 202(c) orders and load growth have pushed many co-op and muni retirements back (from memory). A unit held under 202(c) must keep burning coal, which delays rung 1. CCR ash-pond closure costs of $50-500M+ per site can exceed the value of the rights unless the seller keeps them. None of this is fatal, because there are structural answers: long-term bilateral contracts and leaving the liabilities with the seller.

verdicts.what_survives:
The strongest version is a 'capacity-arbitrage IPP' and does not depend on the full rollup ladder. It turns stranded accredited megawatts into contracted firm capacity at $200-500/kW all-in, against $700-1,000/kW market value for firm gas capacity and $2,000/kW for new build.

How it works:
(a) Target co-op, muni and small-IPP steam units that already sit near firm gas, or have a cheap lateral. AI screening across EIA-860 data, gas pipeline maps and CIR/ELCC data is the per-deal labour lever, and gas-lateral distance should be a top ranking feature.
(b) Do the fuel-switch conversion at the same MW. That keeps the CIRs and needs no queue at all.
(c) Remove the capacity-price risk, the biggest numbers risk, by selling 10-15 year bilateral firm-capacity contracts to data centers or load-serving utilities at ~$200-300/MW-day, or into PJM's proposed long-term reliability backstop procurement. Do not rely on the collar.
(d) Leave CCR and decommissioning liabilities with the seller through an asset-only purchase or a long lease of the switchyard and site.
(e) Only then add aeroderivative or used-frame repowers under replacement-generation or surplus-interconnection rules.

Revised legs:
N 3: works on contracts, fragile at merchant prices.
T 4: rung 1 needs no queue, 12-18 months to first revenue.
C 4: IPP comparables.
A 3: AI is diligence and records lift, not the unlock.
D 3: the CIR is uncopyable per site, but there is no compounding moat across sites beyond scale and contracts.

Total 17/25. Not refuted, but below the 19 pass line. On numbers alone it reads more as an infrastructure/PE rollup than as a venture-scale software-leveraged company.

Not fatal, but the idea fails the bar as pitched (15/25, A below 3). Search note: the shared web-search budget (200 calls) was already used up when this step ran, so nothing below was re-checked today. Facts marked (mem) come from my knowledge to mid-2026 and should be confirmed in a follow-up.

The incumbent problem: the owner already holds the first rung and can climb it alone. A coal-to-gas boiler conversion costs about $50-200/kW, takes 12-18 months, is done in-house, and needs no new interconnection. A co-op or muni that sees capacity clearing at the $333/MW-day cap has every reason to convert the unit itself and keep the capacity revenue, not sell its interconnection rights to a startup. Owners have done exactly this: Big Rivers Electric converted its Green Station coal units to gas in 2022, and Seminole Electric is building a combined-cycle plant at its own coal site (mem).

The long tail the idea targets is mostly not for sale, and not cheap:
(a) Most co-op and muni coal belongs to load-serving G&T co-ops (EKPC, Buckeye, Associated, Big Rivers, Seminole). They need the capacity for their own members.
(b) Many units sit in SERC and other vertically integrated areas with no capacity market. Without a capacity market, a merchant IPP can earn the capacity price only through a bilateral deal with the local utility, which is a monopsony buyer.
(c) Most of PJM's 50-400 MW coal fleet already retired in the 2012-2022 wave. Under PJM rules, capacity interconnection rights lapse about 1 year after deactivation, so the pool of rights-bearing units is small. What remains is mostly owned by PE or IPPs (Talen, Lightstone, GenOn, Homer City/Knighthead, Keystone/Conemaugh owners) (mem).
(d) Sellers price their rights at IPP M&A levels: NRG buying LS Power's roughly 13 GW for about $12B (about $900/kW), Vistra buying Lotus gas plants for about $730/kW, and Constellation buying Calpine (mem). Frontier Group's Bruce Mansfield and Knighthead's Homer City deals show that coal sites now trade as data-center land, not at $0-100/kW.
(e) Funded players already work this exact screen: LS Power, Hull Street, Earthrise, ArcLight/Alpha Gen, Middle River, Carlyle, ECP, plus hyperscalers and data-center developers (Frontier, TeraWulf, Crusoe, Tract). Screening EIA-860 for these units is a few analysts' work, not a throughput bottleneck. So "AI diligence beats PE throughput" is not a moat.

Two corrections to the numbers:
- Capacity accreditation. PJM ELCC for gas steam and combined cycle is roughly 60-79%, so 200 MW nameplate earns about $15-19M a year at the cap, not $24.3M.
- The cap is temporary. The price collar covers only the 2026/27 and 2027/28 auctions, and there is strong political pressure from governors to keep prices low. Converted boilers also burn gas at heat rates of 10,000-11,500 Btu/kWh, so they earn little energy margin.

Gas supply is an unpriced cost: many coal sites need new pipeline laterals ($2-10M+ per mile) and firm transport.

Remediation risk: coal ash (CCR) closure costs can run $100M or more per site. A seller who knows the site better than any AI model will hand that tail risk to whoever bids most eagerly.

verdicts.what_survives:
Revised score: N3 T3 C4 A2 D3 = 15/25. This fails the pass mark (19+ with no leg below 3) because AI does not answer the main killer: sellers already know what their rights are worth, and owners can convert their own boilers.

The strongest surviving version drops "buy the rights cheaply" and becomes the repower partner that brings the scarce hardware. Merge it with the resurrection-fleet idea (20/25): the company owns a fleet of used, refurbished frame and aeroderivative gas turbines (Frame 6B/7EA at about $83-110/kW), kept alive by its AI-built parts library. It installs them at retiring or converted steam sites whose interconnection rights are near the PJM/MISO deadline, building repowered combined cycle that reuses the existing steam turbine, switchyard and rights.

Deal structure: a JV or long-term tolling and capacity-share with the co-op or muni, which keeps the rights and the CCR liabilities. The company owns the turbines and the operating and parts record. This attacks the real scarcity that incumbents cannot buy their way past: turbine slots booked out to 2029-2031, against the 1-year rights clock and the RRI/replacement fast track. The owner cannot do this rung alone, because OEMs will not sell turbines in time. AI does per-unit work: reverse-engineering parts, digitising plant records into heat-balance and repower designs in weeks, and fleet controls tuning that becomes the evidence for capacity accreditation.

The moat is then the turbine fleet plus the parts library plus operating history, not the rights. Outright site purchases happen only where a distressed small IPP or merchant owner is exiting, with CCR liabilities ring-fenced in the seller's estate.

As a standalone company, "Gridright, the rights-buying IPP rollup" is a PE-shaped strategy whose first rung is held by owners and funded players. As a deployment channel for the resurrection fleet, it adds C (ceiling) and D (defensibility) to that idea.

verdicts.fatal_issue: Nothing found is fatal, but the idea fails the pass bar (19+, no leg below 3) on the AI leg. Interconnection rights are a real moat, but what makes them usable is the FERC/PJM rule change (Replacement Generation fast track, surplus interconnection) plus capital. AI shortens none of the gates that set the clock: (1) gas supply, since many coal sites have no firm pipeline capacity and a lateral needs FERC 7(c) or state siting, about 2-4 years; (2) air permits, where a boiler conversion is usually a minor modification but adding a gas turbine plus HRSG is a PSD major-source permit, 12-24 months; (3) the PJM auction calendar, because new capacity earns only after clearing a Base Residual Auction that returns to 3 years forward around 2027, so a site bought in 2027 earns new-build capacity revenue only from the 2030/31 delivery year; (4) gas turbine and HRSG slots, booked to 2029-31; (5) seller-side approvals, since co-op sales need RUS lender consent and muni sales need a public process. The company sits inside all five gates. AI mainly makes diligence cheaper, and that is the per-deal labour the laws say AI does fix. The main killer is competition for sites with sellers pricing in hope. AI answers it only partly. It also faces a competitor the idea leaves out: co-ops can repower their own plants with cheap USDA Empowering Rural America (New ERA) grants and loans (~$9.7B program) instead of selling. At its core this is a well-timed PE-style rollup with AI on top. It is not an AI-native company.
evidence: The web search budget for this turn was used up (limit of 200 shared across agents). I ran no new searches. The points below come from the idea's own citations plus my domain knowledge. They need checking in a follow-up.

Clock gates: FERC accepted PJM's Replacement Generation Resource track in Jan 2026 (cited, https://www.troutmanenergyreport.com/?p=13304). This removes the ~5-year queue wait (https://www.pew.org/de/research-and-analysis/articles/2026/02/09/to-harness-power-plants-unused-capacity-states-can-turn-to-surplus-interconnection-service). It does not remove the pipeline, air-permit, auction-timing or turbine-supply gates.

Turbine slots run to 2029-2031 (https://www.turbomachinerymag.com/view/steam-turbines-gas-turbine-bottleneck-siemens-energy). Rung 2, repowered combined cycle, therefore cannot reach revenue in 2 years unless the company sources used or aeroderivative units, which is plausible but limited in supply.

Capacity price risk: the $333/MW-day cap and the $175 floor came from a settlement covering only the 2026/27 and 2027/28 auctions. Later prices depend on PJM reform and political pressure from governors. Accredited capacity is also lower than nameplate: under PJM's ELCC method, gas-steam units are derated well below nameplate, so a 200 MW unit earns less than the $24M a year claimed (estimate ~$15-19M).
A coal-to-gas steam unit runs at a poor heat rate (~10,000-11,500 Btu/kWh). Energy margins are thin and capacity revenue carries the economics, which concentrates the regulatory price risk.

Homer City (https://abcnews.go.com/amp/Technology/wireStory/pennsylvanias-largest-coal-fired-power-plant-now-retired-120412657) shows that well-funded players (Knighthead) and hyperscaler demand are already pricing retiring sites as data-center campuses. That raises asking prices ('sellers price in hope').

Capital close: the first site needs $20-50M equity plus project debt, and the debt has to be raised before any operating history. That is feasible for an infrastructure-fund-backed team, but heavy for a YC-stage company.

Revised scores: N 4 (high site-level IRR from conversion against capacity prices, but capacity revenue is ELCC-derated and price-cap dependent); T 3 (buying an operating, still-running unit gives revenue in under 2 years, but new-build or repowered capacity revenue arrives 2029-30); C 4 (Vistra, Talen and Constellation comparables); A 2 (AI lowers diligence and engineering labour but answers no gate and only partly answers the site-competition killer); D 3 (rights cannot be copied once owned, but each site is won in an open auction against better-capitalised buyers, and the data flywheel is weak). Total 16.
verdicts.what_survives: Strongest version: buy still-operating, retirement-noticed 50-400 MW steam units that already have pipeline gas or co-firing capability. That avoids the pipeline lateral gate and gives the company energy and capacity revenue on day one from the existing capacity commitments. Gas-convert under a minor air-permit modification inside PJM's one-year rights-retention window. Structure deals as liability assumption plus earn-out, using the AI liability/CCR (coal-ash rule) pricing, so seller hope is converted into contingent payments rather than upfront price. Prefer sellers who cannot use New ERA money, meaning munis and small IPPs rather than co-ops. Rungs 2-3 (combined cycle and behind-the-meter data-center loads under surplus interconnection) come later, once turbines are available around 2029-31. As a business this can hold up as a $1B+ mid-cap IPP rollup with a real permission moat. As a YC company it fails the bar: AI is an efficiency layer, not what makes the pain solvable, and it does not shorten the gates. To pass, AI would need to own a gate. The best candidate is making accreditation evidence the product: control retrofits plus telemetry that lift ELCC or ramp performance and earn measurably higher accredited capacity per MW. That would make the AI-tuned fleet the thing that earns the extra revenue, not just the deal-sourcing tool.

idea.name: Gridiron: a resurrection fleet for data-centre electrical gear
idea.sector: Data-centre physical infrastructure: medium-voltage power train (transformers, switchgear, UPS, gensets)
idea.one_liner: Buy decommissioned and stranded transformers, switchgear, UPS and gensets. Use AI to turn each unit back into a full test-and-design record, remanufacture it, put our own warranty and captive insurance behind it, and rent it out by the MW-month to AI builders stuck in 2-4 year equipment queues.
idea.what_it_owns: The fleet itself: re-certified MV power blocks (transformer + switchgear + UPS skids, 2.5-10 MW each). Also the per-serial-number evidence record (test history, telemetry, remanufacture traceability), our own NRTL field-evaluation and warranty history, and the captive insurance cell that carries the risk. Customers rent, Gridiron keeps title. This is the United Rentals / Aggreko position for the scarcest iron in AI.
idea.wedge_first_revenue: Bridge power-train rentals to neoclouds, crypto-to-AI conversions and second-tier colos that hold a utility feed but have no transformer or switchgear for 18-36 months. First deal: rent 2-4 re-certified 2.5-3 MVA pad-mount transformer + switchgear skids at a premium MW-month rate on 12-36 month terms. Supply comes from retired enterprise data centres, closed factories, crypto mines and utility surplus yards. First revenue in about 6-9 months: rewind and re-test is weeks, and a UL field label is per-unit labour, not an 18-month queue.
idea.ladder: 1) Pad-mount and dry-type distribution transformers plus LV switchgear (easiest to test and field-label). 2) UPS and battery plant, and diesel/gas gensets (UL 2200 field evaluation). 3) MV switchgear and substation transformers up to 30-80 MVA, with an owned rewind and repair shop: the scarce physical capacity, and our 'foundry'. 4) A standard rentable '10 MW power block' API: any site gets a characterised, insured power train in weeks. 5) Asset-backed securitisation of the rental book once there are 24-36 months of availability history (P10). At that point the company is a lessor-operator of grid-edge iron with the lowest cost of capital in the category.
idea.numbers: Lead times: distribution transformers about 2 years and large power transformers about 2-4 years (80-210 weeks); transformer prices up about 60-80% since 2020 (NREL, Major Drivers of Long-Term Distribution Transformer Demand, Feb 2024, https://www.nrel.gov/docs/fy24osti/87653.pdf; figures from prior knowledge, verify). Demand: hyperscaler capex about $400B in 2025 and est. $550-650B in 2026. Electrical M&E is est. 15-25% of the roughly $10-13M/MW all-in build cost, so about $2-3M/MW (est.). At est. 30-50 GW of US data-centre additions to 2030, the electrical-gear pool is roughly $60-150B (est.). Unit economics (est.): a used 2.5 MVA transformer plus switchgear skid costs about $80-150k to acquire, plus $60-120k to remanufacture and test, against roughly $400-700k new with a 2-year wait. Renting at est. $8-15k per MW-month gives a 12-24 month payback, and 3-5 rental cycles over a 30-year life. Capital: est. $15-30M seed/A for the first 100 MW of fleet plus a rewind shop. Asset debt after 24 months. Time to $100M revenue: est. 4-5 years (about 700-1,000 MW on rent). Ceiling comps: United Rentals ($16.1B 2025 revenue, $22.5B fleet at OEC, per project notes); Aggreko (taken private by TDR/I Squared for about GBP 2.3B in 2021, prior knowledge); Eaton bought Fibrebond, a modular power-enclosure maker, for about $1.4B in 2025 (prior knowledge, verify).
idea.ai_role: AI does the decompiling (P1/P12). From nameplates, scanned drawings, dissolved-gas analysis, frequency-response analysis, power-factor/tan-delta tests, thermal imaging and the unit's history, it rebuilds a technical data package and a remaining-life model for each serial number. That is the same 'AI-built parts library' move as the turbine fleet, applied to the scarcest gear in AI. It also: (a) checks substitutions, so any customer's single-line diagram can be built from whatever units sit in inventory (the 'hardware lockfile', P7); (b) drafts the NRTL field-evaluation dossier, the arc-flash study and commissioning paperwork per unit, which is per-unit labour that AI does fix; (c) runs fleet telemetry that turns operating hours into evidence an insurer can price (P9/P14); (d) triages thousands of liquidation listings, auctions and utility surplus lists to find mispriced units.
idea.main_killer: Two problems. First, supply: good used MV gear is thin, utilities hoard spares, and once the gear shortage is publicised, brokers 'price in hope' (law 2). Second, buyers: hyperscalers will not put refurbished gear in a Tier III critical path, and the shortage may ease by 2028-29 once Hitachi, Siemens Energy, Eaton and Hyundai capacity comes online.
idea.ai_answer_to_killer: Supply: do not depend on finding used units. Use AI-designed rewinds and re-cores of failed and obsolete transformers (the core tank and steel are reusable, while windings, bushings and tap changers are the failure points), so failed units become feedstock. AI-based remanufacture design is what turns scrap transformers into fleet. Buyers: start with the many neoclouds, sovereign-AI builds and behind-the-meter projects that price speed over pedigree. Give our own availability guarantee backed by a captive insurer, priced from per-unit telemetry (the HSB 1866 model, P14), so the customer never carries refurbishment risk. Shortage ending: rental fleets earn more when demand is correlated and lumpy (P3, break 3). After the shortage the same fleet serves emergency replacement, bridge-to-grid, outage cover and utility storm reserves, which is the Aggreko business, and the owned rewind shop stays scarce capacity either way.
idea.competitors: OEM service arms (Hitachi Energy, Siemens Energy, ABB, Eaton, Schneider). Transformer remanufacturers and dealers (SPX Transformer Solutions, Sunbelt Solomon (owned by Sunbelt Rentals / Ashtead), Maddox Transformer, ELSCO). Rental power (Aggreko, Sunbelt Rentals Power & HVAC, United Rentals Power, APR Energy). Modular power makers (Fibrebond/Eaton, Vertiv modular). Funding for each not verified in this run.
idea.principles_used: P1 (decompiling hardware is now cheap), P3 (owned pooled capacity rented through an API: 'EC2 for iron'), P7 (substitution resolver), P9/P14 (fleet evidence plus captive risk makes us our own gate), P10 (securitisation sets cost of capital), P12 (break the OEM aftermarket lock).

verdicts.fatal_issue: The rental price is capped by the option to just buy a remanufactured unit now, and at rung 1 that option already exists, so the $8-15k per MW-month rate and the 12-24 month payback cannot hold. (1) The '2-4 year queue' is the wrong number for the wedge. Pad-mount transformers up to 5 MVA quote 40-65 weeks, dry-type up to 2 MVA 20-32 weeks and 15 kV switchgear 52-72 weeks (Terrapin 2026). The 2-4 year figures (power transformers 128 weeks, GSUs 144-160+ weeks) apply only to rung 3. (2) The scarcity premium at rung 1 is already arbitraged. Maddox ships remanufactured distribution units in 1-4 weeks from 'thousands' in stock across five US shops, pays 'up to five times scrap value' for feedstock (so it sets the used-supply price) and sells at 10-40% under new. Sunbelt Solomon (42 locations, sold to TJC in July 2026) does transformers and switchgear, new and remanufactured, up to about 85 MVA. (3) The arithmetic: 2.5 MW at $8-15k per MW-month is $240-450k a year. That is more than buying a new 2.5 MVA transformer plus LV switchboard (my estimate is about $200-380k in 2026, from prior knowledge; the idea's $400-700k looks inflated), and far more than buying from Maddox. On 12-36 month terms, a rational neocloud buys. Rental is only worth it near normal rental yields: the UR benchmark is roughly 60-70% of OEC a year on short rentals, and long-term rentals run lower at about 3%/month of OEC (prior knowledge). On roughly $200k of remanufactured value per 2.5 MW that is about $2-3.5k per MW-month, 3-5x below the plan. (4) At that rate, $100M of revenue needs about 2,800 MW on rent, roughly 3,700 MW of fleet, or about $300M+ of capex for distribution-class gear alone. That is a commodity rental business against Sunbelt Rentals, United Rentals and Aggreko, which already rent transformers and gensets, and Ashtead and UR have far cheaper debt. (5) AI does not answer this killer. AI decompiling and paperwork cut per-unit labour, but rewinds and remanufacturing are routine at Maddox, Solomon, ELSCO and the OEM shops without AI. AI cannot remove the customer's buy option, which is what sets the price. AI-designed rewinds of failed units add feedstock but do not create pricing power, because the incumbents rewind too.

verdicts.fatal_issue: Nothing is fatal, but as pitched the idea fails the rubric at about 17/25. Four problems. (1) The product is wrong. Renting gear that gets permanently installed is awkward. A transformer or switchgear lineup feeding a live data hall cannot be taken back at the end of a 12-36 month term without a planned outage or a redundant path. So customers will want to buy, or to lease with a buyout, not rent, and Gridiron's "3-5 rental cycles over 30 years" disappears. (2) Gridiron sits inside a gate. The clock is not set by an NRTL. It is set by the local electrical inspector (AHJ) at each site, applying the NEC reconditioning rules (110.21(A)(2) marking, plus outright bans on reconditioning some equipment, e.g. molded-case breakers under 240.88 and panelboards under 408.8, from memory of NEC 2020/2023), and by the customer's insurer and lender (FM Global-style property insurers, project-finance lenders' independent engineers). AI can draft the evidence package. It cannot make an inspector, an insurer or a hyperscaler accept refurbished gear in a Tier III critical path. (3) The physical bottleneck is rewind-shop capacity and skilled winders, and that does not come up in 6-9 months. (4) Sunbelt Solomon (Ashtead), the OEM service arms, and utility spare pools (EEI STEP, Grid Assurance) already hold the reman, rental and spares position, so D and C are capped. None of this kills the idea outright. The fix is to change the product shape (see what_survives).

NREL, Major Drivers of Long-Term Distribution Transformer Demand (Feb 2024): distribution transformer lead times of about 2 years and price rises of about 60-80% since 2020 support the shortage premise. https://www.nrel.gov/docs/fy24osti/87653.pdf

NFPA 70 (NEC) 2020/2023 added rules for reconditioned equipment: 110.21(A)(2) requires reconditioned gear to carry the reconditioner's name and date, and some articles ban reconditioning outright (from memory: molded-case breakers 240.88, panelboards 408.8, ground-fault protection 230.95). Acceptance is up to the local inspector at each site. This is a per-site gate, not a per-unit task. https://www.nfpa.org/codes-and-standards/nfpa-70-standard-development/70 (verify article numbers)

NEMA's reconditioned-equipment guidance lists which electrical equipment it considers suitable for reconditioning and which it does not. OEMs use it to discourage refurbished gear in critical facilities. https://www.nema.org/standards/view/evaluating-water-damaged-electrical-equipment (related NEMA reconditioning policy, verify)

Sunbelt Solomon (Ashtead/Sunbelt Rentals) already runs a large inventory of new, remanufactured and rental transformers with its own rewind and repair shops, and is a direct incumbent with a much larger balance sheet. https://www.solomoncorp.com (prior knowledge)

Utility spare-transformer pools already exist for the storm and emergency reserve rung: EEI's Spare Transformer Equipment Program (STEP) and Grid Assurance (backed by utilities). This weakens the post-shortage Aggreko fallback for large power transformers. https://www.eei.org and https://gridassurance.com (prior knowledge)

Aggreko and United Rentals Power already rent temporary transformers and switchgear for events, outages and commissioning, so the true temporary-rental use case is contested. https://www.aggreko.com (prior knowledge)

The neocloud bottleneck is usually utility interconnection and MW allocation, not the low-voltage power train. Many sites with a utility feed get the MV/LV transformer from the utility. That shrinks the pool of buyers who 'have a feed but no transformer' (judgment, unverified).
verdicts.what_survives:
The idea is not refuted. Revised scores: N 3, T 4, C 4, A 3, D 3 = 17, below the 19 pass line but with no fatal issue. Strongest version: "Gridiron" as an owned, insured remanufacturing capacity and power-block leasing company, not a rental shop for permanently installed gear.
(1) Sell or lease with a buyout, don't rent. Offer 5-10 year availability-guaranteed leases on characterised power blocks (transformer + LV switchgear, 2.5-5 MVA), with title held and a buyout option. That is an equipment-lease and asset-backed-securities book, not 3-5 rental cycles.
(2) True rental only where gear really comes back: commissioning and energisation bridges, swaps during upgrades, failure replacement under a service contract, and mobile substations. Gridiron's edge there is speed: a characterised spare in days.
(3) Stay out of the hyperscaler critical path. Sell to neoclouds, crypto-to-AI conversions, behind-the-meter gas-powered campuses (which pair naturally with the turbine resurrection fleet as one 'firm power + power train' block) and industrial users. These buyers have accepting inspectors and insurers and price speed over pedigree.
(4) The gate answer. Gridiron cannot be the inspector, but it can make inspector and insurer acceptance routine. Do only equipment classes the NEC allows to be reconditioned (transformers, switchboards, LV/MV power breakers). Ship each unit with a reconditioning mark, an NRTL field label and an AI-drafted test and remaining-life dossier, and attach an availability warranty backed by a captive insurer, so an inspector, lender or insurer signs off without new risk.
(5) The defensible core is scarce physical capacity plus evidence: an owned rewind and re-core shop (later 30-80 MVA), where AI rebuilds the design for undocumented and obsolete units, turning scrap cores into feedstock and cutting engineering hours per rewind. Add per-serial-number telemetry and failure history to price the warranty. AI is a real efficiency lever (design reconstruction, dossier drafting, sourcing triage) but not the enabler, so A stays at 3.
To reach 19+: (a) show the AI re-core cuts rewind turnaround or engineering cost by 2x or more against Sunbelt Solomon or OEM shops; (b) win early acceptance of the warranty from a lender or insurer; (c) bundle with the turbine fleet into one owned 'island power plant' product, which lifts C and D. Biggest unresolved risk: lead times ease around 2028-29 and Sunbelt Solomon or the OEMs match on price with bigger balance sheets.
